articles.title: As Social Security fund runs dry, some Republicans say it’s time to raise taxes
articles.summary: For decades, Washington has replayed the same fight over taming the soaring national debt: Democrats cite a need for more taxes. Republicans refuse. And anyo...
articles.body:
For decades, Washington has replayed the same fight over taming the soaring national debt: Democrats cite a need for more taxes. Republicans refuse. And anyone who suggests cutting the biggest source of spending - federal retirement benefits - gets attacked.

But a coming crisis in Social Security appears to be pushing at least a few Republicans off the GOP's long-standing pledge never to raise taxes.

This summer, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) joined Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts) in proposing to raise the payroll tax cap so people with higher incomes pay more into the program. Now the idea is emerging as an acceptable fix among other GOP lawmakers, including Rep. Tom Cole (Oklahoma), the influential chair of the House Appropriations Committee.

"We've got too many people who say, 'Well, we have to stay within the current income level or stay at the current tax rate,'" Cole said in an interview. "I'm willing to look at the tax rate. I am willing to raise the amount of income through tax."

The rare GOP concessions on taxes come as lawmakers begin to confront a Social Security shortfall so large and so imminent that the party's traditional demand for curtailing benefits is unlikely to suffice. In just six years, millions of Social Security recipients will absorb a 22 percent cut in benefits unless lawmakers provide an immediate infusion of nearly $500 billion.

"Twenty or thirty years ago," when the shortfall was far in the future, "you could come up with a straight-faced solution" that solved the problem entirely by cutting future benefits, said Charles Blahous, a senior research strategist at George Mason University's Mercatus Center who served from 2010 to 2015 as the Republican public trustee for Social Security.

Now the problem is so big and urgent, Blahous said, "I don't think you can look at it with a straight face and not do all of the above."

Grover Norquist, founder of Americans for Tax Reform and the longtime enforcer of Republican anti-tax orthodoxy, dismissed the crack in party discipline, arguing that Republicans should stick to demanding spending cuts. Otherwise, he said, they risk infuriating voters already angry about the high cost of living.

"When Republicans say no to tax increases, they win. When they say yes to tax increases, they lose," Norquist said. "They don't get spending cuts - at all. And, they get smeared in the next election."

But Cole, at least, said he thinks the political blowback from Social Security benefit cuts would be far worse than a comprehensive solution that includes raising taxes.

"I love Grover. But … you've got to deal with Social Security," Cole said. "And believe me, you'll have a lot bigger problem if it goes bankrupt than you'll have keeping it whole, because people will feel cheated."

Created during the Great Depression, Social Security provides monthly cash benefits to more than 70 million Americans. It is the single largest program in the $7.4 trillion federal budget, paying out $1.7 trillion this year, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. (Medicare is a close second at $1.3 trillion.)

The program is funded by a payroll tax on wages up to a "cap" of $184,500 a year, with workers and employers each paying 6.2 percent. Workers who pay into the system can receive monthly checks as early as age 62, though the full retirement age is 67.

For years, annual tax collections exceeded the cost of benefits, allowing the program to amass a surplus known as the Social Security trust fund. As the baby boom generation retired, however, the math flipped: Social Security now pays out far more than it collects and is draining the trust fund to make up the difference.

The trust fund is projected to run dry in 2032. At that point, Social Security would have to rely solely on incoming tax collections - meaning monthly checks would shrink by $440 on average unless Congress acts, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington think tank.

Closing the shortfall would require $459 billion in cuts or fresh revenue in 2033 alone, according to the BPC - and the sum would grow larger every year.

That relentless math persuaded Moreno, a former car dealership owner who rode into office with President Donald Trump's endorsement in 2024, to break ranks with his party on tax hikes. In his proposal with Warren, Moreno calls for eliminating the payroll tax cap so highly compensated workers pay the tax on their entire income.

"Why should a middle-class nurse pay a larger share of her paycheck than a wealthy corporate lawyer?" Moreno and Warren wrote in an op-ed for the New York Times, noting that one recent poll found that 62 percent of Republicans support lifting the cap. "This is doubly unfair in an economy in which top earners' wages, over time, have pulled far ahead of those of the average worker."

Moreno declined an interview request. His spokesperson Reagan McCarthy said in an email: "Sen. Moreno promised Ohioans he would fight for them in DC and make sure they get the benefits they were promised and that's exactly why he's leading this effort."

Removing the cap without increasing benefits for high-earning workers would close more than half the program's shortfall, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a nonpartisan group focused on deficit reduction. Blahous and others have cautioned against that approach, saying it would sever the connection between contributions and benefits that makes Social Security different from - and more popular than - other social welfare programs.

Uncapping the payroll tax alone would push the top marginal federal tax rate over 50 percent, according to the Manhattan Institute, a conservative think tank.

Some Democrats would go further. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) argues not only for lifting the payroll cap but also for taxing the investment income of wealthy households and closing a loophole that lets business owners shrink their personal tax bills.

That proposal, which would fall entirely on the backs of the wealthy, would raise enough cash to fully fund Social Security for at least 75 years, according to a 2023 estimate by the program's chief actuary.

The historic link between contributions and benefits makes changing Social Security politically perilous. That's why many in Congress want negotiations to be outsourced to a bipartisan commission or advisory board.

Cole has introduced one of several proposals to form such a panel. He argues that more tax revenue, including from raising the payroll tax cap, "ought to certainly be on the table" alongside adjustments that would reduce future spending, such as raising the retirement age.

A third GOP lawmaker, Rep. Lloyd K. Smucker of Pennsylvania, has also said he sees more tax revenue as part of a Social Security fix. "You'll probably have to do something on the payroll half of the money being paid into the system," Smucker told Roll Call last week.

Smucker said lawmakers should also consider means testing, so benefits are reduced for the wealthy while low-income retirees are protected. Smucker's office did not respond to requests for comment.

Though raising taxes is unpopular among Republicans, it has long been part of bipartisan plans to solve the Social Security puzzle. In 1983, President Ronald Reagan, a Republican, and House Speaker Tip O'Neill, a Democrat, saved the program from its last bout with insolvency, agreeing to a mix of solutions that included increasing payroll taxes and gradually raising the retirement age.

In 2005, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-South Carolina) argued for raising the payroll cap and trimming benefits. Weeks later, President George W. Bush said he was open to a "variety of options," though his plan to curtail future benefits for all but low-income retirees and divert some tax dollars to new private retirement accounts was dismissed by Congress.

And in 2010, several Republicans on a commission formed by President Barack Obama voted in favor of a debt-reduction plan that included raising the payroll cap, raising the retirement age to 69 and trimming benefits for wealthy retirees. The plan offered by the so-called Bowles-Simpson commission never received a vote in Congress.

Sen. Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) was among the commission's yes votes. Crapo now serves as chairman of the powerful Senate Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over both taxes and Social Security.

At a committee hearing last month, Crapo said the Bowles-Simpson plan "has informed subsequent Social Security solvency discussions." His office did not respond to questions about his current position on tax hikes.

Another hallmark of Social Security reform has been deep involvement by the White House. Cole said he has urged Trump to take on the hard work of fixing the program, calling it a potential "crowning achievement." Since Trump is not running for office again, he could "do it with no political risk," Cole said, adding, "I think he'll get enormous political credit for it."

But while Trump has warned Republicans not to cut "a single penny from Medicare or Social Security," he has not said how he would raise the vast sums needed to bolster the programs' deteriorating finances.

White House spokesperson Liz Huston did not respond to questions about fixing the program, saying via email only that "there will be zero reductions to Social Security payments" under Trump's leadership.

articles.title: Montes Mínguez, portavoz del PSOE, sobre si se entera que hay financiación irregular en su partido: “Lo dejaría el día de mañana”

articles.summary: La política ha argumentado que la formación que lidera Pedro Sánchez “se ha desnudado” ante el juez
articles.body: La portavoz del PSOE, Montse Mínguez, ha concedido una entrevista en RNE y que ha recogido Europa Press en la que ha hablado sobre los casos de corrupción que se están investigando en su partido y sobre el auge de la ultraderecha. Mínguez ha sostenido que ella “no sería portavoz” y que dejaría el cargo “el día de mañana” si se descubre financiación ilegal dentro de su partido. Además, ha sostenido que la formación que lidera Sánchez no se ha financiado de manera irregular, al contrario de, como ha mencionado la socialista, el Partido Popular, el cual es el único partido condenado por financiación ilegal. Por otro lado, la portavoz ha declarado que el PSOE se ha “desnudado” delante del juez, haciendo referencia a que no ha escondido nada, incluso que ha entregado un documento de excel con sus cuentas bancarias. Mínguez ha argumentado que el caso por el que se está juzgando al PSOE no tiene ni punto de comparación con los casos de corrupción del PP, pero que hay gente que ha querido “empatar” la situación de ambos partidos. “Aquí no hay caso Bárcenas ni Gürtel”, ha remarcado. Al ser preguntada por el caso en el que se está investigando a Leire Díez, exmilitante socialista conocida como la “fontanera” del PSOE, Mínguez ha defendido que ya no forma parte de su partido, mientras que los imputados del PP siguen dentro del mismo. “Pregunte a Leire lo que hacía”, le ha recomendado a la periodista y ha añadido que “son contundentes ante cualquier sospecha e indicio”. ”Cuando algo huele en el PSOE sale por la puerta”, ha recalcado. Por último, Mínguez se ha pronunciado sobre un posible adelanto electoral y sobre la estrategia de la oposición. La portavoz ha señalado que “se está intentando atacar por la manera personal de desgastar la figura del presidente porque de otra manera no pueden. No han podido superar lo que pasó en 2023”, en cuanto a los casos que rodean a la familia del presidente. Mínguez ha añadido que no sabe si se adelantarán las elecciones de 2027, pero que cuando Sánchez crea que se deban celebrar las elecciones él estará preparado.

articles.title: Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch is leaving amid tensions with Trump
articles.summary: Lonnie G. Bunch III will step down from his position as head of the sprawling Smithsonian Institution by the end of the year, he said Tuesday.
articles.body: Lonnie G. Bunch III will step down from his position as head of the sprawling Smithsonian Institution by the end of the year, he said Tuesday. He will depart at a vulnerable time for the institution, which includes dozens of museums along with libraries, research centers and the National Zoo. While the Smithsonian has traditionally operated independently of the party in power, the Trump administration has repeatedly criticized how the institution portrays America’s past. Last week, the Interior Department threatened to cut off support, alleging that Smithsonian facilities present a “radical ideology” that weakens “shared American identity.” Bunch, who has worked at the Smithsonian for 38 years, said in a statement that his retirement came “with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude.” “I have spent nearly half of my life working at and being part of the Smithsonian family, and what a privilege it has been,” said Bunch, who became secretary in 2019. “There is no place like the Smithsonian — it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together.” A person familiar with the situation told NBC News there was no pressure from the Regents — the board that leads the museums — for Bunch to resign. Bunch, the first Black person and first historian to lead the institution, has said he would have retired a year ago but felt he had to stay to defend the institution from the White House attacks, the person said. He told friends after seeing last week’s letter from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum that he believed now was the time to step down and assist in the transition to new leadership, the person said. Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as chancellor of the Smithsonian, praised Bunch in a statement. “From his days as a young curator at the National Air and Space and American History Museums through his tenure as the founding director of the African American History and Culture Museum and culminating in his distinguished service for the past seven years in the Smithsonian’s top job, Secretary Bunch has pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story,” Roberts said. “The Regents, and the Smithsonian, have benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership. We look forward to working with him in the coming months to ensure a smooth transition for his successor.” The person familiar said the Regents are forming a search committee and considering inside candidates to lead the Smithsonian during the transition, and Bunch told them he would stay on for three or four months to ease the changeover. President Donald Trump took aim at the Smithsonian shortly after beginning his second term, issuing an executive order in March 2025 that directed Vice President JD Vance to eliminate “improper, divisive, or anti-American” ideology from the museum’s programs. “Once widely respected as a symbol of American excellence and a global icon of cultural achievement, the Smithsonian Institution has, in recent years, come under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology,” the order said. “This shift has promoted narratives that portray American and Western values as inherently harmful and oppressive,” it alleged. Because of his position as vice president, Vance is a member of the Smithsonian Board of Regents, whose other members include Roberts, members of Congress and members of the public. In August last year, Trump wrote on social media that he’d also asked “my attorneys” to conduct a review of Smithsonian museums, because they’re focused too much on “how bad Slavery was.” “The Smithsonian is OUT OF CONTROL, where everything discussed is how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been — Nothing about Success, nothing about Brightness, nothing about the Future,” he wrote in the Truth Social post. Vance criticized Bunch’s leadership at a Regents meeting several months ago, two people who attended the meeting told NBC. The White House continued attacking the institution on Independence Day. As the country was celebrating its 250th anniversary, the White House Domestic Policy Council issued a report blasting Smithsonian leaders as radical activists who cannot be trusted. “The Smithsonian Institution, and the National Museum of American History in particular, under its current leadership and current interpretive ideology, cannot be trusted to tell America’s story honestly and in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic,” the report said. In an unrelated interview that aired the next day on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Bunch said “the notion of being a more perfect union, not the perfect union, is really what motivates me.” “America’s greatest strength, it’s not running away from its history, but it’s understanding how that history shaped us and continues to shape us,” he said. Megan Brand contributed reporting.

articles.title: Trump posthumously awards Medal of Freedom to 9/11 hero Welles Crowther
articles.summary: President Trump posthumously awarded to Welles Crowther, an equities trader and volunteer firefighter who died working to save lives on 9/11, the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks. Trump presented the honor to Crowther’s mother and sister during the Steel Across America event commemorating the anniversary of…
articles.body:
President Trump posthumously awarded to Welles Crowther, an equities trader and volunteer firefighter who died working to save lives on 9/11, the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

Trump presented the honor to Crowther’s mother and sister during the Steel Across America event commemorating the anniversary of the attacks at the Ellipse near the White House.

“This means the world to me, my daughters, Paige and Honor, and our entire family. This will be treasured for generations to come,” Crowther’s mother, Alison, said at the event.

Welles Crowther, 24, was working in the south tower at the World Trade Center and helped usher people to safety before he was killed when the tower collapsed.

His family has since established the Red Bandana Project, a social and emotional learning curriculum.

Tuesday’s event featured a 16,900-pound steel beam that was recovered from the rubble at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan following the attacks. The Tunnel to Towers Foundation brought it to the White House.

Trump is slated to mark the 25th anniversary Friday at the Pentagon, where he will deliver remarks.

Vice President Vance will travel to Ground Zero in New York City for a memorial service where he will join former Presidents Clinton, George W. Bush, Obama and Biden.

articles.title: Families of 9/11 victims' message to Mamdani: 'Please do not come' to memorial ceremony
articles.summary: A 101,000-signature petition delivered to City Hall demands Mayor Zohran Mamdani skip the 25th anniversary 9/11 memorial service on Friday.
articles.body: A coalition of 9/11 family members, first responders, and elected officials gathered on the steps of City Hall on Tuesday to deliver a message to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani: stay away from this year's Sept. 11 memorial service. "This mayor is not serving us," Charles Wolf, who lost his wife on 9/11, said at a noon news conference. "He's serving himself. We are asking respectfully that he not show up." "Even though there is going to be other politicians there, these are the politicians that helped us push beneficial laws through and literally held our hand during that time," Wolf continued. "Mayor Mamdani has not shown any of that, none of it. He just wants to be there because he wants to be there." "So we are asking him to respect the fact that that trauma is revived during the ceremony. It is a private ceremony. It is not a public ceremony. Mayor Mamdani, please do not come." TRUMP POSTHUMOUSLY AWARDS MEDAL OF FREEDOM TO 9/11'S ‘MAN IN RED BANDANA’ New York City Council Member Vickie Paladino, a staunch, outspoken conservative, said she was leading organizers and family members into City Hall to formally deliver a petition with more than 101,000 signatures directly to the mayor’s office ahead of Friday’s 25th anniversary service. "I am demanding that he not show his face at that sacred ground," Paladino said. "He does not belong there." "We the people do not care for Zohran Mamdani – 101,000 names is not a drop in the bucket. Do not, Zohran Mamdani, take us New Yorkers for granted. We were there that day. The sky looked very similar to this. Stay put. Stay in City Hall and promote your propaganda." Organized by Giovanni Galante — whose wife, Grace, was killed in the Sept. 11 attacks — the petition asks that the sacred anniversary remain a solemn, distraction-free day of mourning rather than a backdrop for political presence. "We don't believe in what he believes in, and we really want us to be left alone," Galante said. "This 25th anniversary is for victims and survivors to blend in and pray that day for all the families — not have a circus around us." MAMDANI UNDER FIRE AFTER SYMBOLIC 9/11 PEN GOES TO FORMER AL QAEDA DEFENSE LAWYER The sentiment was echoed by other grieving family members who stressed that the Sept. 11 memorial service is a private, sacred space for victims' relatives to gather in peace. "If we feel that we don't want someone at our world-class memorial museum that's sacred and hallowed, we feel that that person should respect our wishes," said Monica Iken, whose husband, Michael, was killed in the attacks. "He didn't go to the 20th … so I don't know why he's so adamant about going to this one when we just ask that he just respect us from 7 to 11 and let us have our mourning." The objections stem directly from the mayor’s current policy positions, political associations, and key appointments, according to the speakers at the news conference. Cheri Sparacio, whose husband, Tom, was killed in the South Tower, said the petition was not about the mayor's background or faith, but his public actions. She noted Mamdani’s appointment of chief counsel Ramzi Kassem — who previously represented individuals accused of terror ties — and his past ties to figures who have downplayed terror threats. "That is what we object to," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP NYC Council Member Joann Ariola, also a Republican, accused the mayor of attempting to deflect from the families' concerns with performative announcements leading up to the event, rebuking the fact he has surrounded himself with advisers holding views hostile to core American values. "Other politicians will be there, no one will speak — it is about the survivors and about those who were murdered that day," Ariola said. "Mayor Mamdani, for once, listen to your constituents and not your influencers and stay away from an event, a ceremonial commemoration of the lives that were lost on 9/11."

articles.title: Smithsonian head Lonnie Bunch to retire amid allegations of far-left woke messaging at museums
articles.summary: Lonnie Bunch III announced his retirement from the Smithsonian Institution amid an escalating clash with the Trump administration over museum leadership.
articles.body: The head of the Smithsonian Institution announced his retirement Tuesday, stepping down amid an escalating clash with the Trump administration over the leadership and direction of the nation’s museums. Lonnie Bunch III, who has led the Smithsonian since 2019 and was the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, said he will leave the post by the end of the year. "It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement from the Smithsonian," Bunch said in a press release. "I have spent nearly half of my life working at and being part of the Smithsonian family, and what a privilege it has been. There is no place like the Smithsonian — it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together." SMITHSONIAN SHOWDOWN INTENSIFIES AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ISSUES A STARK NEW WARNING "I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward," he added. Bunch’s departure comes as the Trump administration has intensified scrutiny of the Smithsonian, accusing its leadership of allowing progressive ideology to shape its presentation of American history and raising concerns about potential violations of federal nondiscrimination law. In a letter recently made public by the Department of the Interior, the administration said the Smithsonian leadership’s "institutional culture may have resulted in significant violations of Federal antidiscrimination law," including allegedly creating a hostile work environment and allocating opportunities, funding and other benefits based on race, ethnicity and other protected characteristics. The letter did not include specific evidence of illegal activity, and the Department of the Interior did not provide further information when previously reached for comment by Fox News Digital. The administration warned that federal agencies could withdraw certain forms of support if its concerns are not addressed, saying an "appropriate response" from the Smithsonian "must likewise address executive leadership and institutional ideology." The pressure follows a 2025 executive order directing officials to seek the removal of what the administration called "improper ideology" from the Smithsonian. SMITHSONIAN'S TAXPAYER FUNDS FACE CHOPPING BLOCK AS GOP DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY FOR 'WOKE' HISTORY Bunch became the Smithsonian’s 14th secretary in June 2019, making him the first African American and first historian to hold the position. He previously led the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, serving as its founding director from 2005 through its opening in 2016. Bunch first joined the Smithsonian in 1978 and has spent nearly four decades at the institution, apart from a period when he served as president of the Chicago Historical Society. Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as chancellor of the Smithsonian, praised Bunch’s tenure and said the institution would work with him to ensure a smooth transition. "From his days as a young curator at the National Air and Space and American History Museums through his tenure as the founding director of the African American History and Culture Museum and culminating in his distinguished service for the past seven years in the Smithsonian’s top job, Secretary Bunch has pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story," Roberts said. articles.title: JD Vance is betraying his fellow Marines
articles.summary: Why is Vice President JD Vance claiming the Iran War isn’t a war?
articles.body:
When President Trump put JD Vance on the ticket, it made sense to me and many other veterans. Here was a guy who literally epitomized the vast majority of Global War on Terrorism vets. He took time out of his life to serve, worked in a non-combat unit but went into a war zone, served with honor, and got out and did amazing things in the civilian world.

This guy was us, and in some ways the best of us. I didn’t agree with his politics, but I felt that if anyone in the Trump administration would be there for active service members, the millions of veterans in this country, it would be him.

But Vance, out of loyalty to MAGA talking points, decided that he was going to do the worst thing that a veteran can do — throw his fellow service members under the bus.

Vance last week decided to prance out into the White House Press Briefing Room and declare that the Iran war was in fact, not a war . Of course, this denial of the obvious only benefits one person — his boss, who decided to plunge into a conflict that even Vance was opposed to initially, has been beset by sagging poll numbers and a public animosity toward yet another foreign intervention.

If Vance was initially opposed to the war but now has to sell it to the American people ahead of what is looking like a bloodbath in the midterms, then so be it. But to insist that it is not an actual war is a stab in the back, not just to the men and women who have been engaged in combat for the last six plus months, but to veterans in general.

Take the widow of Alex Klinner, an Air Force Major who was killed by Iran. Libby Klinner has struggled to get combat-related benefits that are owed to her because the Pentagon wouldn’t classify her husband’s death as killed in action. Only after having the news media directly confront Vance on the issue, did the U.S. military move to take care of a Gold Star widow.

It should not have come to that, but here we are. And it goes further than the families of those killed. Being in a combat zone is a very stressful thing to deal with. And many service members, going way back, struggle to come forward because of a minimization of what they went through by fellow service members, their commands, or the veteran community at large.

In the aftermath of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars, Marine veterans like Vance and me found themselves in an awkward spot. We went to a war zone, took indirect fire, went outside the wire, interacted with Iraqis, came across improvised explosive devices, went on patrols, drove across the country in military convoys, flew in helicopters between bases, and counted the days until we could go home.

But there was one particular thing that Marines like Vance and me did not do. We didn’t shoot anyone. That was a big deal, because only when actually firing your weapon could you qualify for a Combat Action Ribbon — the benchmark among Marines for determining whether you were actually a combat veteran or not. Although I don’t really care about ribbons or medals, the fallout of the years has had a negative effect on veterans of those wars.

Many veterans have been reluctant to call themselves combat veterans out of fear that they might be challenged by fellow veterans. This meant that many veterans would refuse to accept that they had been through a pretty serious experience just by being in a war zone. I went on patrols, was stationed on the Syrian border checking for bombs, convoyed all over the Al-Anbar province and came across improvised explosive devices, took fire from rocket-propelled grenades, took rifle fire and flew all over the country in a helicopter but when I came home, I insisted that what I went through was not combat because the military told me to.

It took meeting Medal of Honor recipient Florent Groberg at a work conference to get into my head that maybe my experience was more serious than I or the military wanted it to be. This applies to many veterans who have been shamed into not dealing with their military experiences the way they should. Vance should understand this because he went through it.

Which brings us to Iran. At least for Global War on Terror veterans, we had the benefit of these conflicts being called wars. The current service members who are out on ships or stationed at airbases now don’t have that protection because it makes Trump look bad.

With hundreds injured and thousands more who are sure to deal with the aftermath of such a stressful experience, it would be nice if the one guy who should understand them actually stood up for them instead of turning against them.

Joslin Joseph is a recipient of the Military Reporters and Editors award for Best Commentary-Opinion. A graduate of Harvard and Ohio State, he is a Marine veteran who served in Iraq. He currently lives in Anaheim, Calif.

articles.body:
Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch III announced Tuesday he will be stepping down from his role amid Trump administration disputes with the museum complex over how it presents American history.

Bunch, 73, is the Smithsonian Institution’s first Black leader and founder of its National Museum of African American History and Culture. He’s served as the world’s largest museum complex’s top official for more than seven years.

The secretary plans to leave his post by the end of the year, according to a Tuesday afternoon statement from the Smithsonian.

“It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement from the Smithsonian,” Bunch said in the statement. “I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.”

News of Bunch’s retirement comes less than a week after the Trump administration threatened to cut the Smithsonian’s funding and end its partnerships with federal agencies over accusations that the museum complex’s leaders are pushing a “culture of ideological activism” through its exhibits.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Trump adviser Vince Haley included these threats in an Aug. 28 letter to Smithsonian leaders — citing a July White House report identifying what they described as “alarming examples” of “radical ideology” across museum programming.

“Those executive departments and agencies cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership by, for example, loaning artifacts for exhibits, enabling procurement processes and making discretionary grants,” the letter reads.

Bunch told The Washington Post on Tuesday that the administration’s pressure did not influence his decision to step down, adding that he had been considering retirement for roughly a year to spend more time with family.

He further emphasized to the Post that he was still passionate about protecting the Smithsonian’s freedom and autonomy.

“We’re at a time when people are challenging that independence,” he said. “I feel very strongly that it is as independent as we were before, and that I will continue to fight — for as long as I’m in this chair — for the independence of the Smithsonian.”

According to the outlet, he informed the executive committee of the board of regents about his decision to retire last week and planned to stay long enough to ensure “a peaceful transition of power.”

articles.title: Democrats make sharp gains among Latino voters in battleground districts: Poll
articles.summary: A new poll found that Democratic candidates have made notable gains among Latino voters living in battleground House districts since 2024 — gains that could determine control of Congress next year. A new Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision poll shared with Axios shows that Democrats hold a 58 percent advantage on the generic congressional ballot among the fastest-growing swing…
articles.body:
A new poll found that Democratic candidates have made notable gains among Latino voters living in battleground House districts since 2024 — gains that could determine control of Congress next year.

A new Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision poll shared with Axios shows that Democrats hold a 58 percent advantage on the generic congressional ballot among the fastest-growing swing electorate across 17 competitive House districts, with Republicans winning the support of 35 percent of Latino voters.

The poll found that Latino voters in three competitive House races in Texas went from a self-reported 44-44 split on the 2024 presidential race to 56-36 in favor of Democrats going into the midterms.

Latino support for Democrats has also risen in other states, with 57 percent in California saying they will back Democrats compared to 33 percent who say they will back the GOP.

“Latino voters aren’t locked into one party,” Kate Coleman, TelevisaUnivision’s senior vice president, told Axios. “They’re paying close attention and making decisions based on who shows up for them, and how they’re showing up.”

Pollsters found that 11 percent of Latino respondents who said they voted for President Trump in 2024 now back Democratic candidates. The president has seen his support from Latinos sour as he has ramped up his deportation agenda, stoking fear in many Latino neighborhoods.

Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision found that 63 percent of Latino voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the presidency, with 36 percent saying they support his job performance.

His handling of high prices — and the cost of living — also faces 65 percent disapproval from Latino voters, with 62 percent also saying they do not approve of his handling of immigration enforcement and deportations. More than half, 64 percent, of Latino voters disapprove of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

A poll from UnidosUS released in May showed a quarter of Latino voters said they either “probably would not vote for Trump again” or definitely would not back him in the case they “had to do it over again.”

The poll showed at the time that Democrats had not made many gains in the wake of Trump’s unpopularity among Latino voters.

Pew Research Center data showed that Trump’s support among Latino voters improved in 2024, receiving 48 percent of the Latino vote, just short of the 51 percent won by former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The worry among some Democrats is whether the rising tide of democratic socialist victories in the primaries could leave some Latino voters — including those who fled Cuba or Venezuela — with a sour outlook on the party going into November.

The Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision survey was conducted Aug. 6-17 and included 1,500 Latino respondents. The margin of error is 2.5 percentage points.

articles.body:
House Republicans’ campaign arm is adding five candidates to a battleground seat program as election season heats up.

Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.), chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC), in a Tuesday press release unveiled that five candidates in Florida and North Carolina were being included in the MAGA Majority program.

The candidates include four Floridians and one North Carolinian.

Dan Green, Mike Beltran and Scott Singer — in Florida’s 9th, 14th and 25th Congressional Districts, respectively — will challenge Democratic incumbent Florida Reps. Darren Soto, Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz, respectively.

Casey Askar is battling for an open seat in Florida’s 22nd District, as is Jennifer Balkcom in North Carolina’s 11th District.

According to the press release, the MAGA Majority program backs battleground district candidates, aiming “to provide them with the necessary tools to run successful, winning campaigns against their Democrat opponents.”

“House Republicans have an incredible bench of proven leaders who are ready to take the fight to the radical socialists,” Hudson said in the release.

“These candidates have what it takes to win, deliver for their communities, and help us keep America on the path to prosperity and security.”

Republicans are facing an uphill battle in their fight to maintain control of Congress, with the unpopular war in Iran passing the six-month mark, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and Democrats performing well in recent polling on issues like affordability .

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.8 percent on Tuesday afternoon with his disapproval rating at 56.7 percent.

articles.title: Gulf nations race to bypass Hormuz and build defenses as Iran war drags on
articles.summary: ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates - The Persian Gulf nations are building up their own defenses and finding routes around the Strait of Hormuz, officials said,...
articles.body:
Gulf nations race to bypass Hormuz and build defenses as Iran war drags on

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates - The Persian Gulf nations are building up their own defenses and finding routes around the Strait of Hormuz, officials said, as they confront a U.S. war against Iran with no end in sight.

The wealthy countries, known for their stability before the war, have borne the brunt of Tehran's retaliatory attacks.

They are now increasing their spending on security and diversifying their international security partnerships.

Construction on a pipeline in the United Arab Emirates is expanding, while ports in the UAE and Oman that are outside of the Strait of Hormuz are booming, as they become hubs for nations that have no alternative to the narrow waterway, which has largely has been blocked by the war.

President Donald Trump has said in recent days that the U.S. military is helping "millions" of barrels of oil transit the strait, through which about 20 percent of global oil and gas supplies passed before the bombing of Iran started in February.

Despite Trump's claims, maritime tracking companies show that the number of ships passing through the strait has reduced to a trickle.

Today, the main threat facing the Gulf region is "normalization" of the crisis, Majed al-Ansari, spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry of Qatar and an adviser to Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, said Monday.

"It is no longer seen as a temporary crisis with a start and an end date," he said at the Hili Forum, a regional conference in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the UAE. "It is more and more seen as a new normal."

As the Trump administration seeks to impose an economic stranglehold on Iran, a tactic with little precedent of success, officials from the United Arab Emirates and Qatar said at the conference in Abu Dhabi that it is essential for Gulf nations, which have long relied on the United States as their top security partner, to broaden their horizons.

"Strategic autonomy does not mean strategic isolation," said Anwar Gargash, a diplomatic adviser to the president of the UAE. "Our long-standing and trusted partnerships, in particular with the United States, remain an essential part of our security and an important source of strength. The two are complementary, not contradictory."

Gargash said Iran "remains our neighbor, and at some point we will have to find a way to restore what can be restored."

"Geography gives us no alternative to engagement," he added. "But we must distinguish clearly between rebuilding a necessary and functional relationship with Iran and rebuilding the trust that has broken. The first is necessary. The second will be far more difficult."

The remarks by Gargash and other officials underscored the risk to U.S. allies in the Gulf as the Trump administration seeks to impose maximum pain on the Iranian economy, which is deeply intertwined with those of other Gulf nations.

In recent weeks, the U.S. and Iran have traded limited strikes, with the U.S. military on Saturday saying that it hit three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, the country's main oil terminal, after Iran launched missiles toward two U.S. Navy warships.

The Trump administration has signaled that an intensive new military campaign is unlikely and that the president's preference is to use a naval blockade and a bevy of sanctions to impose leverage in hopes of exacting concessions, including an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

But experts have cast doubt on the idea that U.S. economic pressure will force the Iranian regime to capitulate.

Iranian officials have acknowledged the pain of recent sanctions on their economy. But instead of being more willing to negotiate, they have ramped up strikes and bellicose rhetoric.

Al-Ansari, the official from Qatar, which has been helping mediate an end to the war, said that one major roadblock is a "narrative problem," because "if the other party's narrative succeeds, then strategically, they have failed. … Therefore, it makes more sense for them to continue [fighting]."

At this point, it appears that neither the U.S. and Israel nor Iran are willing to be seen as having failed, he said. That creates a major obstacle, he said, to determining "a desired outcome for both parties" to declare the war over.

In that context, al-Ansari said: "Having international forces in the region, having a strategic alliance in the United States, is very important, but it is not enough. Self-sufficiency when it comes to security is the only way forward."

In the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Oman, officials have been able to use ports outside of the Strait of Hormuz - with access to the Arabian Sea and beyond to the Indian Ocean - to continue to export oil and import other goods.

The nations of Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain, which do not have such ports, or land borders that allow them to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, have suffered more acutely.

With a single drone, al-Ansari noted, Iran was able to take out about a critical portion of Qatar's liquefied natural gas supply - which represents 20 percent of the world's overall LNG supply.

The weapons industry is "definitely expanding across the Gulf," said Mohammed Baharoon, director general of B'huth, a Dubai research center, with Gulf nations turning to partners including Ukraine, Turkey and South Korea as they prepare for the future.

"It used to be about defense and deterrence," he said. "But now it is also about offense."

When the UAE deployed a Chinese-made defense system to Bahrain, which has been targeted by barrages of Iranian drones and missiles, there was no objection from the United States, he noted.

"Every country is working on a plan B," said Nasser Hassan Al Shaikh, a businessman, former UAE government official and economist. "We know that life cannot stop."

Especially when it comes to oil, he said, the attitude can be summed up as: "Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. Especially with something as important as oil."

DP World, which runs the massive Jebel Ali Port in Dubai, where traffic has declined dramatically, announced in July that it would build two new deepwater terminals in Fujairah beyond the Strait of Hormuz.

The Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. (ADNOC) is speeding up construction of a 320-mile pipeline that is expected to open next year, while construction of a train line was also accelerated.

Heading toward the UAE's Khorfakkan port on a recent day, lines of trucks snarled along roads cut into a mountain.

The port has seen an influx of traffic, with the number of containers it handles jumping to 70,000 a week from about 8,000 before the war, said Farid Belbouab, the chief executive officer of Gulftainer, the UAE-headquartered global port and logistics solutions provider that operates the port at Khorfakkan.

"We are not saying we are building something to replace Hormuz," he said. "But our role is to drastically reduce the dependence on it."

articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: Dem rebels expose cracks in Jeffries’ House leadership
articles.summary: Jared Golden and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez blindsided Hakeem Jeffries by handing House Republicans a crucial procedural vote with zero warning.
articles.body: Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, may retire from Congress next year with a reputation that is anything but gilded among his fellow Democrats. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., is seeking re-election in a competitive district. But some of her colleagues may consider "MGP" to be notorious if she returns to Capitol Hill in January. The House of Representatives is now out — again — until Sept. 14. That follows a six-week sabbatical over the summer. But were it not for Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, House Republican leaders may have had no other choice but to send members home early a few days ago. The duo committed something close to a parliamentary heresy, handing the GOP the necessary votes on a procedural matter to unlock the floor for the majority. Republicans lacked the votes to do it on their own – had Golden and Gluesenkamp not intervened. JEFFRIES THREATENS 'SERIOUS RESPONSE' AFTER DEMOCRATS HELP GOP ADVANCE ANTI-SOCIALISM VOTE However, the most schismatic betrayal was that neither one briefed Democratic leaders on what they planned to do. Congressional leaders from both sides are never pleased with members who stray from the party line. Especially on a procedural vote, which is almost always the responsibility of the majority to pass. But at the very least, leaders like to be clued in. They might give someone a pass if they understand the reasoning. "Did they give you a heads up that they were going to vote with Republicans on that rule?" asked Fox News' Kelly Phares of House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass. "They did not. They surprised us," answered Clark. Yours truly observed to Rep. Tim Kennedy, D-N.Y., that in politics it’s always best to "stab someone in the front" rather than "in the back." "There’s a lot to be said for that," replied Kennedy. Let’s start with the nature of the dissent by Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez. Most major pieces of legislation in the House need what's called a "rule" before the body can debate the measure. The House must debate and approve a "rule," dictating how much time and what amendments would be in order. The House can’t debate a bill until it first OKs a rule. And except on rare occasions, the majority party is expected to carry the rule. It’s simply something the minority party rarely assists with – except in extreme circumstances. Last week, the House planned to debate a resolution to condemn socialism, green-light the SAVE America Act, maintain the number of justices on the Supreme Court at nine and consider a plan to help the nation’s lobster industry. The House adopted the rule, 210-208. However, five Republicans voted nay on the rule. It’s about the math. Those GOP defections would have killed the rule and frozen the floor for the rest of the week. In fact, the vote may have compelled House Republican leaders to cut everyone loose from Capitol Hill. The House was stalled considering any legislative traffic. TENSIONS ERUPT IN HOUSE HEARING AS GOP ADVANCES ANTI-SOCIALISM RESOLUTION WHILE DEMS RAGE: 'SILLY SEASON' But Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez voted yes, unlocking the floor for the remainder of the week. Democrats seethed at their colleagues for blindsiding them. "The two Democrats who have voted to move a procedural bill forward didn’t do the right thing," said Kennedy. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Clark and House Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., issued a rare, joint condemnation of the dissenting duo. They characterized the revolt "a significant breach of trust," adding it "necessitates a serious response." "It’s a mistake to vote against our caucus. We have to be unified," said Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa. Golden said he voted with Republicans so the House could pass the bill safeguarding Maine’s lobster industry. "It’s about protecting the working-class communities those men and women support. In my district, lobster fishing is the backbone of towns up and down the coast," said Golden. "In some towns, 20 to 40% of residents hold a lobster license." Political observers view the infighting as a misstep for the party ahead of November. "As a member, you should be able to communicate with your leaders and how you intend to vote," said Rep. Susie Lee, D-Nev. "Something was skipped along the way." While some lawmakers blamed Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, others said this was the fault of Jeffries. Others put it on Clark. Still, there were those pinning this on the entire leadership team. Former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., knows something about his own members undercutting him. Republicans stripped McCarthy of the speaker’s gavel nearly three years ago. But the California Republican believes the problem with Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez falls on the shoulder of Jeffries. "You would know who would be the five to eight Democrats who would leverage that [vote]," said McCarthy. "You would have reached out to them." One former Democratic aide noted that it wasn’t even what Jeffries, Clark and Aguilar said in their statement. But it was the very fact that a statement appeared. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., never would have sent a statement. Her leadership power was implicit. Everyone knew not to cross her. Or, if there was an issue, at least have a conversation. HOUSE CONSERVATIVES DERAIL GOP AGENDA IN SAVE AMERICA ACT SHOWDOWN Jeffries has not been the House’s top Democrat in the majority. That could change if Democrats win the House this fall. But McCarthy argued the statement said a lot about Jeffries. "If Hakeem has to put out a statement that he's strong, it's a sign that he is weak," said McCarthy. One senior House Democratic leadership source said rank-and-file members demanded accountability by Jeffries. Golden is done in January. Gluesenkamp Perez has repeatedly defied political gravity in a district which favors President Donald Trump. The source didn’t believe anything Machiavellian was afoot between Democratic leaders and Gluesenkamp Perez. But the source indicated that Gluesenkamp Perez tussling with the Democratic brass probably helps the Washington Democrat back home. Still, some Democrats demanded retribution. "I think there should be consequences. I think at the end of the day, we have a caucus united against what Republicans are trying to do," said Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the Oversight Committee. Actions speak louder than words. Remember that Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez voted against a "rule" in the House. Gluesenkamp Perez appeared at an unrelated meeting of the Rules Committee the next day. During her testimony, Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., the top Democrat on the panel, swiveled around in his chair and sat with his back to his fellow Democrat. Jeffries hoped to turn a corner with the renegades. He spoke briefly with Golden. But had a deeper conversation with Gluesenkamp Perez. "Congresswoman Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and myself were able to talk in a very forward-looking way about how to make sure that we're all on the same page as we approach the midterm elections and beyond," said Jeffries. He indicated that McGovern and Gluesenkamp Perez also talked. But the leader was cryptic when pressed why he even had to issue an admonition. HOUSE DEMOCRAT LASHES OUT WHEN GRILLED ON WHETHER SOCIALIST VICTORIES WOULD THREATEN DEM UNITY "Does that say something about where the Democratic Caucus is and if they follow your leadership?" I pressed Jeffries. "Res ipsa loquitur," answered Jeffries. "That's Latin for ‘the thing speaks for itself.’" Not really. Was the statement just a warning shot as Jeffries tries to flex his muscles in anticipation of becoming speaker and presiding over a Democratic majority next year? Where’s that "serious response" that Democratic leaders spoke of? Some Democrats who are angry about the desertion will demand action. And if Jeffries doesn’t respond forcefully – despite a declaration otherwise – some members may interpret the warning statement as prattle. That said, Democrats need Gluesenkamp Perez to win her district in order to claim the majority. And more specifically, Jeffries needs Gluesenkamp Perez to support him for speaker if Democrats have control next year and the margin is close. articles.title: Major blue state hospital pulls plug on controversial child transgender treatments after DOJ intervention
articles.summary: Mount Sinai, one of New York City's largest hospitals, agreed to stop sex reassignment procedures for minors and allocate $2 million for patient care.
articles.body: One of the largest hospitals in New York City will stop providing sex reassignment procedures to minors after entering an agreement with the Trump administration. Mount Sinai has provided sex reassignment services, which included hormonal therapy and surgeries, to thousands of transgender patients. In 2025, Mount Sinai's Institute for Advanced Medicine reported that its providers saw 4,931 transgender and gender-diverse patients, but the exact number of minors receiving sex reassignment procedures has not been publicly disclosed, according to the hospital's report. "The Department of Justice is committed to holding accountable medical providers that violate federal law and endanger children through so-called gender-affirming care," said Attorney General Todd Blanche. "This agreement puts an end to these practices at Mount Sinai and provides meaningful relief for individuals who have already suffered harm." LARGEST CHILDREN’S HOSPITAL IN US TO OPEN ‘DETRANSITION CLINIC’ AFTER $10M SETTLEMENT WITH TRUMP DOJ, STATE The agreement includes a monetary penalty and requires Mount Sinai to dedicate $2 million to free medical care for people suffering harmful consequences from transgender treatments they received as children. The agreement comes as part of an ongoing Justice Department investigation into hospitals providing such procedures to minors. "A growing number of hospitals, like Mount Sinai, have recognized the medical scandal of sex-rejecting procedures," Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate of the Civil Division said in a statement. "While we are grateful when we secure resolutions to end this discredited practice and protect children, we must not and will not rest in our pursuit of justice for the victims it has left behind." Curbing sex reassignment procedures for minors has been a top priority under the Trump administration. JD VANCE CALLS ON DOJ TO PROSECUTE ALLEGED FRAUD IN TEEN TRANSGENDER TREATMENT Just a week after being sworn into office, President Donald Trump issued an executive order titled "Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation," seeking to defund federal funding for gender reassignment procedures and directing the Justice Department to enforce the nation's female genital mutilation laws and investigate drug-safety violations and potential parental rights violations. The Justice Department's investigation examines potential violations of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the False Claims Act and other federal health care laws, including alleged fraudulent billing practices such as the use of false diagnosis codes to obtain payment from federal health care programs and private insurers, according to the department. The executive order also directed federal agencies to rescind or amend policies that rely on guidance from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH). WPATH, a professional association that develops standards of care for transgender and gender-diverse patients, is being sued by the Federal Trade Commission and several states, which allege the group made false and unsubstantiated claims about the safety, effectiveness and medical necessity of pediatric medical-transition services. The case is pending. COLORADO SUPREME COURT ORDERS CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL TO RESUME GENDER TRANSITION TREATMENTS FOR MINORS WPATH's medical guidelines served as the bedrock for Mount Sinai's medical guidelines for transgender procedures, and Dr. Joshua Safer, executive director of the Mount Sinai Center for Transgender Medicine and Surgery, has co-authored WPATH guidelines. The Justice Department did not release the details of the agreement with Mount Sinai but acknowledged that the hospital "remained cooperative, proactive, and solution-driven" at all times of the investigation. "The settlement is complex, but at its core reflects Mount Sinai’s commitment to safeguarding our patients’ confidential information and protecting our clinicians," Mount Sinai said in a statement to the New York Times. Mount Sinai's settlement is just the latest the Justice Department has reached with major hospitals providing transgender procedures. Texas Children's Hospital, the Cleveland Clinic Foundation and Connecticut Children's Hospital have agreed to halt youth transgender procedures in the past couple of months. articles.title: Socialists praise fatness and ugliness, attack MAHA’s ‘health fascism’
articles.summary: as Americans, we do not share in the socialist vision of desiring our own decline. We shall seek self-improvement and the extension of our species because these are moral goods. We praise beauty because it is right to do so. We promote beauty because we want more of it.
articles.body:
While I was in Provincetown enjoying gorgeous weather and gorgeous people, the socialist left spent the weekend attacking President Trump and the right and the MAHA movement for supposedly promoting health and body “fascism.” That’s because the right wants to empower Americans to eat correctly and be in good shape.

Seriously, I’m not making this up. This was a topic of conversation at their annual gathering in Chicago over the weekend.

As part of a panel on health fascism, participants assailed the notion of being conventionally attractive and healthy as tools of oppression used by the capitalist system to oppress working people and conscript them for the rulers! According to socialist podcaster Beatrice Adler-Bolton, it’s also ableist and racist and productivist — that’s a new one — and so on and so on. Just listen.

Listen closely to what she’s saying: Efforts to support your friends and family members, your neighbors and your countrymen, as they seek to better themselves physically, in terms of their health, are part of a fascist and racist program, according to socialists.

Now look, the United States unfortunately suffers from an epidemic of obesity and ill health, and the many, many Americans who are afflicted with obesity obviously have the same rights and moral worth as everyone else. No one, absolutely no one, on the right is in favor of mistreating people who are overweight. Frankly, other people’s health is none of my business. You live your life, and I’ll live mine. That is the proper ethos for the right.

But I’m sorry, it is not wrong whatsoever to want to help people escape obesity if they are willing, because obesity is associated with all sorts of serious health conditions that can cause premature death. We all understand this when it comes to kids: We want children to be physically active and to eat right, so that they can be fit and healthy. You don’t need to take this to some insane degree, but it’s a good thing generally to promote healthy eating and an active lifestyle, for children and adults.

But no, according to socialists, if we are at all organized around the principle that fitness and health are to be praised and encouraged and celebrated, then we are reproducing some archaic form of oppression .

“The more dysgenic the better.” That right there is the ethos of socialism, I frankly couldn’t put it any better than she did. According to socialism, it is a moral good to be, and to feel, and to look, unwell. To be diseased and obese. To be rotting from the inside out.

It’s not surprising they feel this way. This is what socialist policies would do to our entire society: rot it from the inside out. Under socialism, there is sickness and suffering. Under capitalism, there is beauty and health.

And to be clear, you don’t have to be a fascist to recognize this dynamic, and to prefer beauty. As I said, I spent my Labor Day in Provincetown, catching some sun and enjoying the beaches, surrounded by so many beautiful people. And it’s true that people are beautiful in all their shapes and sizes, and yes, it’s what’s in your head, and in your heart, that counts.

But as Americans, we do not share in the socialist vision of desiring our own decline. We shall seek self-improvement and the extension of our species because these are moral goods. We praise beauty because it is right to do so. We promote beauty because we want more of it. Socialists do not want more beauty. They want more ugliness and despair, and that’s exactly what their policies produce. In fact, misery is the only commodity that socialism produces in excess.

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: ‘South Park’ jabs Trump after Emmy win, changes name to ‘South America’
articles.summary: The animated show “South Park” said Tuesday that the program’s name will be changed to “South America” amid similar renaming efforts by President Trump. “Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA,” co-creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone said in a statement…
articles.body:
The animated show “South Park” said Tuesday that the program’s name will be changed to “South America” amid similar renaming efforts by President Trump.

“Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA,” co-creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone said in a statement Tuesday. “We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount — a Skydance Capitulation.”

Trump signed an executive order in August that would formally change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.” Last year, he signed a similar executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

In the days following the executive orders, Apple Maps and Google Maps began displaying the changed name for both bodies of waters despite criticism from users.

The show’s creators also referenced the $8 billion merger deal the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved last year between Paramount and Skydance. The approval came after a decision by Paramount to settle a lawsuit brought by Trump for $16 million.

Parker and Stone were critical of these moves at the time in the program’s 27th season, with the show’s season premiere depicting the president in bed with Satan. The episode also featured Trump continuously screaming and threatening to sue other characters for hurting his feelings or defying him alongside other administration officials such as Brendan Carr, chair of the FCC.

The show’s official Instagram mocked the president Monday when celebrating an Emmy win for Outstanding Animated Program earlier this week. The post showed an animated Trump character with his pants down holding an Emmy, along with the text, “You finally got your Emmy.”

Trump was nominated for an Emmy twice for NBC’s “The Apprentice” in 2004 and 2005, but lost both times to CBS’s “The Amazing Race.”

The White House did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment.

articles.body: Graham Platner’s replacement in the Maine Senate race suggested the government should be able to take over private property when necessary, appearing to echo socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s housing agenda. Troy Jackson, a Democrat running for the Senate, came under fire for suggesting the government should be able to take over private property when necessary. The comments drew fresh scrutiny to a candidate the Pine Tree State’s GOP chair previously dubbed "Maine’s Mamdani" to Fox News Digital, as debates over government intervention in housing and private ownership gain new attention. "It’s a major issue. The greed that's happening right now in this country that people in mobile home parks are feeling is like something I've never seen," Jackson told a small crowd of residents at Blueberry Ridge Mobile Village, one of several Maine trailer parks where concerns about costs, quality-of-life and ownership arose. MAINE DEMOCRATS CROWN TROY JACKSON AS PLATNER REPLACEMENT AS FRESH SCRUTINY CLOUDS SENATE RESET "The other thing that I do hear a lot about, too, is how [landlords] won't do anything for services. And that is completely unfair and not right. And we have to make that change. I feel strongly that if needed, the state should be able to come in [and] take these places over. Some people will say that that's insane," Jackson told the residents in Wells, the town next to the politically-notable Kennebunkport. "But until the people get the chance to start a co-op or whatever, there should be a way to hold these, so that you don't see private-equity coming in and making the killing on these parks." PROPERTY OWNER ADVOCACY GROUPS PUSH BACK ON MAMDANI'S 'RENTAL RIPOFF REPORT,' PUBLIC DATABASE OF LANDLORDS During his visit, Jackson held up a mason jar of brown water a resident said came from their tap. Jackson said some residents saw their lot rental fees approach $850, adding he once lived at a mobile home park in Aroostook County and understands their plight. "I’m going to add my voice to that every damn day," he said. "I just can't imagine owning a home and feeling the threat that you do daily and getting the squeeze and not being able to afford that." Jackson’s proposal echoes one of the more aggressive elements of Mamdani’s housing agenda: a willingness to use government power to wrest control of troubled properties away from private owners and toward tenants, nonprofits or community stewardship. MAMDANI RIPPED OVER 'FREAK SHOW' NEWS CONFERENCE WHERE EVICTION WAS DECLARED A FORM OF 'VIOLENCE' Like Mamdani, Jackson was endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in his prior unsuccessful gubernatorial primary bid earlier this year. Mamdani’s Block by Block housing plan, released in May, calls for aggressive legal action against negligent landlords and says chronically neglected properties could be transferred to community land trusts, nonprofits or tenants. BERNIE-BACKED SOCIALIST WHO ALLIED WITH PLATNER COULD SUPPLANT HIM ON BALLOT "Through the Open-Door program and by supporting community land trusts, we will remove negligent owners and property managers of buildings suffering from chronic neglect or mired in foreclosure and shift ownership to responsible community stewards," Mamdani said in June. While Mamdani’s more nationally-visible rent-freeze plans are materially different from Jackson’s considerations, they share a common thread: the government should intervene in the housing market when politicians believe pricing or practices are untoward. MAMDANI’S $22 BILLION HOUSING LUNACY PROPOSAL WILL SOCIALIZE THE SKYLINE That commonality led to Jackson being lambasted after the fact. "Another full-on Communist running for office," said Lt. Col. Tony Shaffer [Ret.], a former intelligence officer, posted to X. "Troy Jackson is ready to violate the rights of Mainers because he feels that they make too much money engaging in free market commerce," Shaffer tweeted. "Spoken here like the true Stalinist he is." RESURFACED ASSAULT REPORT PUTS DEM SENATE NOMINEE IN GOP CROSSHAIRS: 'GRAHAM PLATNER 2.0' The Republican National Committee also caught wind of Jackson’s comments, tweeting through their rapid-response arm. "Troy Jackson wants the government to seize private property from Mainers," they wrote. Under Title 10, Section 9094-A, a group of mobile home owners or a residents’ association has the first option to purchase the park and generally has 60 days after notice of an intended sale to submit an offer.
